title: syntax
text:
This module uses spaCy to detect long sentences, stacked clauses, sentences with three or more punctuation-separated sections, passives, and part-of-speech-dependent vocabulary. It also checks noun clusters, nominalizations, actor placement, and phrases whose meaning depends on their position in a sentence. get_nlp downloads and loads the spaCy model.
from fastcore.test import *

title: syntax
text:
Getting the model
Slopometer uses spaCy’s 40MB en_core_web_md pipeline. The md and lg English models share a vocabulary of 684,830 keys and the same tagger and parser architecture. The md model maps that vocabulary to 20,000 shared vectors. The 560MB lg model keeps 342,918 vectors.
The rules use the parse and vocabulary membership, including is_oov in the variation rule. They do not compare vector similarities. The para notebook explains why the proposed similarity-based detectors failed. A future rule that uses similarity would need its own model comparison.
Explosion publishes the model as a wheel on GitHub releases, outside PyPI. Slopometer downloads it separately rather than declaring a direct-URL package dependency. pip install slopometer requires no extra installation command.
model_path first checks for an installed model package. Otherwise, it downloads the model to the user’s XDG cache directory on first use. The cached copy serves projects across virtual environments and survives environment syncs.

The loaded pipeline, one per process, with a tokenizer that splits off a full stop after a capital that follows a lowercase letter or digit, and that reads id, im, wed and whats as words

CI restores the model cache with actions/cache. The examples do not test a fresh download. get_nlp loads the pipeline once per process. Subsequent calls return that pipeline without reloading it.
get_nlp changes two things in spaCy’s tokenizer. Each lets a full stop after certain words end a sentence. spaCy keeps the full stop on a word that ends in a capital after a lowercase letter or digit, such as NaN. or LaTeX.. get_nlp splits it off. spaCy also reads id, im, wed and whats as contractions without their apostrophe. It splits “user id.” into i and d.. get_nlp reads these four as words. The tokenizer still leaves the full stop on an initial such as “J.” and on an abbreviation such as “vs.”:

nlp = get_nlp()
test_eq([t.text for t in nlp.tokenizer("NaN. LaTeX. 3D. id. J. vs. I'd")], ['NaN', '.', 'LaTeX', '.', '3D', '.', 'id', '.', 'J.', 'vs.', 'I', "'d"])
test_eq([s.text for s in nlp('No running result is ever NaN. Callers get the user id. Pass it on.').sents], ['No running result is ever NaN.', 'Callers get the user id.', 'Pass it on.'])

title: syntax
text:
Reading a parse
The rules use these spaCy token attributes:

pos_ is the part of speech, such as NOUN, VERB, ADJ, or ADV.
lemma_ is the dictionary form. It lets a rule match both “leverages” and “leveraged” with one entry.
dep_ and head describe the token’s grammatical relation to another token. For example, nsubj marks a subject and dobj an object.

The parser also finds sentence boundaries. Splitting on periods would mishandle abbreviations such as “e.g.” and version strings such as “v3.8.0”.
spaCy 101 introduces these concepts. The labels relate to Universal Dependencies, although spaCy’s English models use ClearNLP labels. Chapters 17-18 of Speech and Language Processing explain statistical parsing. Parse errors can cause both missed findings and false positives.

doc = get_nlp()('The gateway never kills an unresponsive kernel.')
L((t.text, t.pos_, t.lemma_, t.dep_, t.head.text) for t in doc)

title: syntax
text:
Sentence load
ASD-STE100 limits descriptive sentences to 25 words and procedural sentences to 20. find_sent_len uses 25 words, excluding punctuation. It adds one weight point per extra word when the sentence also contains at least two clauses. A single-clause enumeration can exceed the cap without a finding.
_n_clauses starts at one and counts these additions:

Each subordinate clause labelled advcl or ccomp.
Each coordinated verb with its own subject. “The kernel gains ports and clients see restarting” counts as two clauses. “Reads stdin, writes to the terminal, sees the same directory” does not add clauses.

Relative clauses such as “a small program that starts fast” do not increase the count. find_clauses flags counts of four or more, with one weight point per clause beyond three.

find_tacked_semi gives a semicolon a weight of 4 when both sides contain a subject attached to a verb. It excludes semicolons inside parentheses, such as citation separators. Lists of noun phrases or participles also pass.

def find_tacked_semi(
    sent

Semicolons joining two independent clauses; serial semicolons and citations pass


Check the list and citation that the old rule misclassified, alongside a tacked-on clause:

nosemi = ['Decided, dropped, or still open; merged, blocked, or awaiting review; a task with nobody named.',
    'The dimensions were settled long ago (SummEval; Fabbri et al., 2021).']
for s in nosemi: test_eq(find_tacked_semi(list(get_nlp()(s).sents)[0]), [])
semi = find_tacked_semi(list(get_nlp()("Say it is open; an honest answer is status too.").sents)[0])
test_eq([f.weight for f in semi], [4])
semi

[[4] semi_splice (tell 1, splices): ';']


A short sentence can still tack several clauses on with commas. “Inside brackets, a space separates items, and a run of tokens with no spaces between them is one item” has 19 words and two clauses. Neither find_sent_len nor find_clauses flags it.
find_sections flags sentences with three or more sections. The weight is one point for each section beyond two. A section ends at a comma, semicolon, colon, em or en dash, or spaced hyphen. A parenthesis adds a section, except inside a list item. Punctuation inside parentheses does not end a section.
List items stay in one section. A comma is a list separator when the items after it have no subject of their own and include a coordinator such as “and” or “or”. Three or more items without subjects also form a list without a coordinator, as in “the target function, the interpreter, the package versions”. A list at the start of a sentence can be the sentence’s subject. spaCy then parses the last item as the subject, as in “Printing, piping, and prompts therefore work exactly as if nothing was in between”. find_sections keeps such a list together when its earlier items have no verbs. Text inside parentheses does not count when deciding whether an item has a subject or a verb. A comma after an opening phrase with no verb, such as “Inside brackets,”, ends a section if the rest of the sentence has a verb. A semicolon ends a section only where find_tacked_semi flags it.

Sentences that punctuation splits into three or more sections, escalating per extra section


Check a noun list, the verb-phrase list in enum, and the semicolon examples above, alongside the bracket sentence:

lists = ['I keep dogs, cats, and birds.', "A server's name includes everything that could change an answer: the target function, the interpreter, the package versions.",

find_sections(tacked)

find_tacked_and flags “, and” when the clause after it has its own subject. Its weight of 3 matches find_conseq’s weight for “, so”. find_sections flags such a join only in a sentence with three or more sections.
The subject test relies on spaCy’s parse and has three known false positives. The rule does not try to avoid them:

A list that forms the sentence’s subject, such as “Printing, piping, and prompts therefore work exactly as if nothing was in between.” spaCy makes the last item the subject of the verb.
A list of clauses, such as “how the code maps onto the world, why the code is the way it is, and how it can be sensibly extended.” Each item has its own subject.
A relative clause after “and”, such as “and construct statements that were never in the text.” The test counts the relative clause’s subject.

Passive voice
“The file is deleted” omits who deletes it. find_passive flags subjects labelled nsubjpass. Its findings weigh 0. Reports list them, but they add nothing to the score.
The assertion below checks spaCy’s labels. A model change that renamed nsubjpass would otherwise disable this rule without an error.

title: syntax
text:
Vocabulary judged by the parse
Some words are inappropriate only in particular uses. “The impact was small” uses a noun. “This impacts performance” uses the verb where “affects” would do. “The fix landed” leaves the reader to infer whether it merged, committed, or released.
find_verb_banned checks part of speech and lemma. It excludes tokens after a hyphen, such as the end of “aviation-shaped”.
find_intensifiers flags “simply”, “merely”, and “effortlessly” as adverbs. It excludes “just” because the same part-of-speech tag covers both minimization (“it just works”) and time (“just released”).

title: syntax
text:
Noun clusters and nominalizations
In “kernel connection state model update”, readers must work out which noun modifies which. find_noun_cluster flags runs containing at least three common nouns and increases the weight for each extra noun. Proper nouns do not count toward the threshold. “New York City subway” passes.
A nominalization expresses an action as a noun: “make a decision” instead of “decide”. find_nominalization checks for a light verb with a derived noun as its object. It suggests a verb from a fixed mapping, such as “assess” for “perform an assessment”.

title: syntax
text:
Actor placement
Joseph Williams’s Style: Toward Clarity and Grace recommends making the doer the subject and the action the verb. Tell 17 covers two ways prose can obscure the doer:

Artifact-as-agent credits a document or change with its author’s action: “this PR introduces”.
Recipient-as-subject describes what the beneficiary receives: “the kernel gains fresh ports via the new process”.

find_artifact_agent requires an authorship artifact as subject and a verb from its crediting list. “The parser rejects malformed input” passes because the parser performs that operation.
find_recipient_subject flags “gain” and “receive” when they have a subject. It flags “get” only with a “via” or “through” phrase.

test_eq(find_artifact_agent(list(get_nlp()('The parser rejects malformed input.').sents)[0]), [])

[[3] recipient_subject (tell 23, recipient-as-subject): 'gains']


A third way gives an act to something that cannot perform it. “The positions decide the result’s shape” credits a value with the caller’s choice. “A single position removes its axis” credits it with what the function does.
find_inert_mind flags a common noun that is the subject of a verb from _mind_verbs, acts that need a mind such as decide, own and prefer. These findings belong to tell 17, because a person made that choice. find_inert_act flags the same subjects with a verb from _act_verbs, physical or deliberate acts such as carry, stamp and remove, under tell 10. Its findings weigh 2, against 3 for find_inert_mind. Nouns in _people and _runners pass with any verb: people and roles such as user and author, and components that run such as parser, server and function.

The lists started from seed words and grew with en_core_web_lg vector neighbours, reviewed by hand. The rules resolve that and who relative clauses to their head noun, and skip other pronouns, proper nouns, inline code and nouns capitalised mid-sentence, because they cannot judge what those refer to. A capitalised noun mid-sentence is usually a tool or API name, such as “Scrub” below. Nouns that act in one project and not in another, such as rule and operator, stay off _runners and give false positives. Quoted mentions give false positives too. for s in actors: test_eq(inert(s), [])
fs = [f for s in inert_sents for f in inert(s)]
test_eq([(f.tell, f.weight) for f in fs], [(17, 3), (10, 2), (10, 2), (10, 2), (17, 3), (10, 2), (17, 3)])

text:
Sentence-anchored patterns
Position matters for some phrases. “This section describes” announces content at the start of a sentence, but “the part this section describes” has another purpose. sent_rule can restrict a phrase list to sentence starts.
The phrase rules cover throat-clearing, today’s-world openers, announce-then-deliver, not-X-but-Y, teasers, and appraisal preambles. find_rhetorical separately flags sentences ending in a question mark.
The not-X-but-Y rule limits its matches to patterns such as “isn’t just a”. It leaves contrasts such as “not thread-safe, but lockable” alone because they can state useful constraints.

title: typesafe
text:
TypeSafe’s Jev model reads a state and answers typed questions about it with probabilities. It generates no text. This module calls its HTTP API. noul builds a yes/no question, systemone sends one request, and ask_nouls returns the probability of yes for each question.
The functions read the API key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY. A request sends its state and questions to TypeSafe’s servers and costs $0.042 per million input tokens.
from fastcore.test import *

title: typesafe
text:
Questions
A Noul is TypeSafe’s name for a yes/no question. Jev answers it with the probability that the answer is yes. instructions holds the question. It can be a string, or a dict that holds the question beside the data it asks about. true and false say what counts as each answer. Each can be a string, a dict or a list.


source

noul
def noul(
    instructions, # The yes/no question: a string, or a dict or list that holds the question beside its data
    true:NoneType=None, # What counts as yes: a string, dict or list
    false:NoneType=None, # What counts as no: a string, dict or list
):
A Noul question, which Jev answers with the probability of yes


A question with no criteria has two fields:

q = noul('Is this message about billing?')
test_eq(q, dict(type='noul', instructions='Is this message about billing?'))
q

A dict keeps the text being judged apart from the question about it. The question names the field in backticks:

q = noul(dict(message='How long do refunds take?', question='Is `message` a refund request?'),
    true='The customer asks for their money back.', false='The customer asks about the refund policy.')
test_eq(q['criteria'], {'true': 'The customer asks for their money back.', 'false': 'The customer asks about the refund policy.'})
q

title: typesafe
text:
Requests
systemone posts one request. Jev reads state once and answers every question against it. Put questions that share a state in one request. A request must fit 64,000 tokens in total. state plus any one question must fit 32,000.
systemone waits and tries again after a 429 response, which means the rate limit was reached, or a 529, which means TypeSafe is overloaded. Any other error raises RuntimeError with TypeSafe’s explanation.

title: segment
text:
Rules read prose, but slopometer’s input is markdown: READMEs, docstrings rendered from notebooks, PR text, chat responses. Segmentation turns a markdown document into typed blocks (heading, list item, prose paragraph) that remember where they came from, discards fenced code entirely, and blanks inline code so that lexical rules never fire on identifiers. Every downstream stage depends on the position bookkeeping here: a finding is only useful if it can point back at the exact file offset it came from.

from fastcore.test import *

A README-shaped fixture exercises everything segmentation must handle: headings, prose with inline code, a fenced block that must vanish, and a bullet list. It reappears throughout the later notebooks, and by the scoring notebook the meter reads it end to end.

SAMPLE = """# widget

A tool for widgets. Call `enhance()` to start.

```python
enhance(x)  # code is never scored
```

Install it:

    pip install widget

## Features

widget leverages a robust paradigm to deliver results.
It parses the config, then it writes the output.

- fast startup
- fast shutdown
- fast restarts
"""

Segmentation delegates block recognition to mdhtml, whose blocks function with nested=True reports the type, source line span and depth of every block, including the paragraphs inside list items and other containers. Segmentation keeps headings and paragraphs. A paragraph that starts with a list marker becomes an item. Other paragraphs become prose, including an item’s later paragraphs. Everything else drops: code blocks and fences, pipe tables, raw HTML, thematic breaks, and block quotes with everything inside them, since a quotation is not the author’s prose. A block’s text starts at its first non-space character. Indented paragraphs inside list items therefore keep the round-trip property. One class of junk needs handling before the parse. The mdhtml dialect renders out-of-subset tags such as iframe as literal text, on purpose, for paste safety. A scorer sees junk where the dialect sees text, and a regex therefore blanks every iframe span first, replacing each character with a space and keeping every newline. Offsets survive both steps. Each block records the offset its text starts at, which makes rebasing a finding onto file positions a single addition.


source

segment
def segment(
    doc
):
Split markdown doc into typed Blocks that keep their character offsets

Block
def Block(
    kind, # 'heading', 'item', or 'prose'
    txt, # The block's text, sliced verbatim from the document after iframe blanking
    start, # Character offset of the block in the document
):



blocks = segment(SAMPLE)
blocks

[<heading @0: '# widget'>, <prose @10: 'A tool for widgets. Call `enhance()` to start.'>, <prose @108: 'Install it:'>, <heading @145: '## Features'>, <prose @158: 'widget leverages a robust paradigm to deliver re'>, <item @263: '- fast startup'>, <item @278: '- fast shutdown'>, <item @294: '- fast restarts'>]


The round-trip property is the contract every later stage leans on: a block’s text is the document’s own text at the block’s offset. The fixture’s fenced block is gone, and nothing else is.

for b in blocks: test_eq(SAMPLE[b.start:b.start+len(b.txt)], b.txt)
assert 'enhance(x)' not in ' '.join(blocks.attrgot('txt'))
assert 'pip install' not in ' '.join(blocks.attrgot('txt'))
len(blocks)

8


A list item keeps its wrapped lines and any later paragraphs. A nested item is an item too. A quote inside an item still drops:

items = '- fast startup\n  that wraps\n\n  A second paragraph.\n\n  > quoted voice\n\n  - nested item\n- fast shutdown\n'
ib = segment(items)
for b in ib: test_eq(items[b.start:b.start+len(b.txt)], b.txt)
test_eq(ib.attrgot('kind'), ['item', 'prose', 'item', 'item'])
ib

Inline code is exempt from every lexical rule: a function named enhance is not a style violation, and write_docs itself requires code symbols in backticks. Deleting the span would shift every offset after it, and that breaks the round-trip property. Filling the span with X characters removes the words and keeps the geometry, and the capitalized dummy token also preserves sentence boundaries: a space-blanked symbol at a sentence start would make the parser merge two sentences. All other markup becomes spaces: emphasis markers, link brackets and targets, HTML tags, footnote labels and math. A URL is an address, not prose, and link text keeps the sentence readable on its own. mdhtml.inlines decides which characters are text and which are code, with the parser that renders the document. A finding’s offsets stay valid in the scrubbed text and in the original alike.


source

scrub
def scrub(
    txt
):
Keep txt’s plain text, fill its inline code with X, and turn all other markup into spaces, keeping every offset unchanged



scrubbed = scrub(blocks[1].txt)

title: lexicon
text: These rules match words, phrases, punctuation, and Markdown emphasis in scrubbed text. They cover banned vocabulary, hedges, fillers, tacked-on clauses, and consequence joins. Findings include plain replacements where available. The rules use regexes without linguistic analysis.

title: lexicon
text:
Sources and related tools
Vale runs YAML-defined prose style rules. write-good checks English prose for passive voice, weasel words, and cliches. proselint implements usage advice from writers including Strunk, White, and Garner. Its authors describe the approach in “proselint: the linting of science prose, and the science of prose linting”.
Slopometer implements its own rules to produce weighted findings, write_docs tell numbers, character spans for edits, and a score. It does not wrap those linters or use Vale’s engine or packages.
The vocabulary combines write_docs with entries adapted from the GOV.UK words-to-avoid list. It contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

text:
Sentences
The model judges sentences, so sentences splits a document into them. It reads the paragraphs and list items that segment returns. Headings are left out, and segment has already dropped fenced code, tables and block quotes. spaCy finds the sentence boundaries in each line of the scrubbed text, where inline code cannot confuse it. Each Sent holds the sentence on one line as a reader sees it. Inline code stays. Link targets and emphasis markers are removed, since scrubbing turned them into spaces. It also keeps its offsets in the document and the index of its paragraph.
Fragments of fewer than min_words words are skipped. Most are list items such as “fast startup”, which have no verb to judge.

Each run shuffles the examples with its run number as the seed. With thinking off, runs of one identical prompt give nearly identical answers, and repeating them finds nothing new. title: features
text:
Burstiness
The Goh-Barabasi burstiness parameter is (s - m) / (s + m), where s is the standard deviation and m the mean. Here it measures variation in sentence lengths. Uniform lengths give a value near -1. The value is zero when the standard deviation equals the mean and positive when it exceeds the mean.
Uniform sentence lengths can occur in both repetitive writing and clear reference prose. Burstiness alone is not a quality rule. flattest_window locates the consecutive sentences with the lowest length variation for closer review.

    "Prompt asking for an `H` or `F` verdict on each of `sents`"
    ex = '\n\n'.join(f'Hard: {h}\nPlain: {p}' for h,p in pairs)
    ok = '\n'.join(f'Fine: {s}' for s in fine)
    doc = '\n'.join(f'[{i}] {s}' for i,s in enumerate(sents))
    return f"""Some sentences make the reader stop and work out what really happened and who did it. Each example below gives a hard sentence and a plain version of the same fact.

{ex}

These sentences are fine as they stand.

{ok}

Judge each numbered sentence below in the same way. Answer with one line per sentence, in the form `12 H` for a hard sentence or `12 F` for a fine one, and nothing else.

{doc}"""


print(judge_prompt(['The parser reads the file.', 'Offsets ride in each row.']))


from fastcore.test import *

survey runs judge several times for each model, all in parallel, and keeps an error as a string so that one failing model does not stop the rest. tally counts the hard sentences a model found, the fine sentences it wrongly called hard, and the sentences it gave no verdict for. Model names are fastllm vendor paths such as openai/gpt-6-luna.

KEYS = dict(anthropic=os.environ.get('ANTHROPIC_KEY'))
@delegates(acomplete)
async def judge(model, sents, timeout=450, **kwargs):
    "`model`'s verdicts on `sents`, with the seconds taken"
    t = time.time()
    c = await asyncio.wait_for(acomplete(mk_msgs([judge_prompt(sents)]), model, api_key=KEYS.get(model.split('/')[0]), **kwargs), timeout)
    return parse_verdicts(contents(c).text), round(time.time()-t, 1)

def tally(verdicts, labelled):
    "Group A sentences found, group B sentences wrongly flagged, and sentences with no verdict; rows with no group count in neither"
    a,b = [{i for i,r in enumerate(labelled) if r['group']==g} for g in 'AB']
    said = {i for i,v in verdicts.items() if v}
    return dict(found=len(said&a), wrong=len(said&b), missing=len(labelled)-len(verdicts))

@delegates(judge)
async def survey(models, labelled, n=3, **kwargs):
    "Run `judge` `n` times per model in parallel; one result list per model, with errors kept as strings"
    sents = [r['text'] for r in labelled]
    async def one(m):
        try:
            v,s = await judge(m, sents, **kwargs)
            return dict(tally(v, labelled), secs=s, verdicts=v)
        except Exception as e: return dict(error=f'{type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:150]}')
    res = await asyncio.gather(*[one(m) for m in models for _ in range(n)])
    return {m: res[i*n:(i+1)*n] for i,m in enumerate(models)}

title: judge
text:
Jev
TypeSafe’s Jev model answers a yes/no question with a probability and generates no text. This section asks it whether a sentence fits one of two example groups. slopometer/judge_groups.txt holds the groups. Group A holds sentences of the hard kind. Group B holds plain sentences, some of them unrelated to the rest. The question names the groups only as grammar_group_a and grammar_group_b, so that it describes no fault.

from slopometer.typesafe import *
from slopometer.segment import scrub
from slopometer.syntax import get_nlp


from slopometer.ai import groups
ga,gb = groups()
ga[:3], gb[:3]

A long sentence can hold several clauses, and only one of them may be hard to follow. Every group A example is a single short clause. clauses splits a sentence into its subject-and-verb clauses, so that Jev can judge each one against examples of the same size:

_cut = {'conj', 'advcl', 'parataxis', 'cc', 'mark', 'punct', 'appos', 'relcl', 'acl'}
def clauses(txt):
    "Each subject-and-verb clause of `txt`, without the clauses joined to it; `[txt]` when it has none"
    d,res = get_nlp()(scrub(txt)),[]
    def walk(t, keep, top=False):
        keep.add(t.i)
        for c in t.children:
            if not (top and c.dep_ in _cut): walk(c, keep)
    for v in d:
        subs = [c for c in v.children if c.dep_ in ('nsubj', 'nsubjpass')]
        if not subs or v.pos_ not in ('VERB', 'AUX'): continue
        keep = set()
        walk(v, keep, True)
        for s in subs: walk(s, keep)
        ids,out = sorted(keep),''
        for a,b in zip(ids, ids[1:]+[None]):
            out += txt[d[a].idx:d[a].idx+len(d[a].text)]
            if b is not None: out += d[a].whitespace_ if b == a+1 else ' '
        res.append(out.strip())
    return res or [txt]


cs = clauses('Rows carry their source, so any experiment can slice by it later.')
test_eq(cs[0], 'Rows carry their source')
cs

Each question builder returns the Noul questions for one labelled row. sent_q asks about the sentence alone. nbr_q adds the sentences before and after it as separate named fields. clause_q asks one question per clause and shows the full sentence beside it. In each, the field name in the question says which text Jev must judge.

JQ = 'Does `{}` fit in `grammar_group_a`, grammatically?'
def sent_q(r, drows): return [noul(dict(sentence=r['text'], question=JQ.format('sentence')))]
def nbr_q(r, drows):
    nb = lambda k: drows[r['i']+k]['text'] if 0 <= r['i']+k < len(drows) else None
    ins = dict(sentence_before=nb(-1), sentence_to_judge=r['text'], sentence_after=nb(1), question=JQ.format('sentence_to_judge'))
    return [noul({k: v for k,v in ins.items() if v is not None})]
def clause_q(r, drows):
    return [noul(dict(full_sentence=r['text'], clause_to_judge=c, question=JQ.format('clause_to_judge'))) for c in clauses(r['text'])]


row = dict(i=0, text='Rows carry their source, so any experiment can slice by it later.')
test_eq(len(clause_q(row, [row])), 2)
clause_q(row, [row])[0]

jev_probs sends one request per document, with the two groups as the shared state. A row’s probability is the highest that any of its questions received. rank_score is the chance that a hard row gets a higher probability than a fine one. It is 0.5 for a random scorer and 1.0 for a perfect one. flagged counts the hard rows found and the fine rows wrongly flagged at a threshold.

def jev_probs(labelled, mkqs, state):
    "Jev's probability that each row fits group A: the highest over the questions `mkqs(row, doc_rows)` builds"
    res = {}
    for d in dict.fromkeys(r['doc'] for r in labelled):
        drows = [r for r in labelled if r['doc']==d]
        ans = ask_nouls(state, {f"s{r['i']}_{k}": q for r in drows for k,q in enumerate(mkqs(r, drows))})
        for r in drows: res[d, r['i']] = max(v for k,v in ans.items() if k.startswith(f"s{r['i']}_"))
    return [res[r['doc'], r['i']] for r in labelled]

def rank_score(ps, labelled):
    "Chance that a group A row gets a higher probability than a group B row, counting a tie as half"
    h,f = [[p for p,r in zip(ps, labelled) if r['group']==x] for x in 'AB']
    return round(sum((x>y) + 0.5*(x==y) for x in h for y in f)/(len(h)*len(f)), 3)

def flagged(ps, labelled, thr=0.7):
    "Group A rows found and group B rows wrongly flagged above `thr`"
    return tuple(sum(p>thr and r['group']==x for p,r in zip(ps, labelled)) for x in 'AB')


lab = [dict(group='A'), dict(group='B'), dict(group='A'), dict(group=None)]
test_eq(rank_score([0.9, 0.2, 0.2, 0.9], lab), 0.75)
test_eq(flagged([0.9, 0.8, 0.2, 0.9], lab), (1, 1))

The cell calls a paid API, so the docs build does not run it:

state = dict(grammar_group_a=ga, grammar_group_b=gb)
dev,holdout = (rows.filter(lambda r: r['split']==s) for s in ('dev', 'holdout'))
{f.__name__: (rank_score(ps, dev), flagged(ps, dev)) for f in (sent_q, nbr_q, clause_q) for ps in [jev_probs(dev, f, state)]}

title: rewrite
text:
Markdown in reading order
A docstring is Markdown. md_parts lists what a reader of its prose sees, in order, as pairs. Each sentence of a paragraph or list item comes as a Sent paired with the list marker in front of it, such as - or 2.. The marker is an empty string when the sentence does not start a list item. A heading, block quote, code block or table comes as None paired with its text. The model needs these to follow the document, but it is not asked to rewrite them.


source

md_parts
def md_parts(
    txt
):
Markdown txt in reading order as pairs: a Sent with its list marker, or None with the text of a heading, block quote, code block, table or YAML front matter


This docstring text has a heading, a block quote, a numbered list with a two-line item, a link, and a fenced block:

MD = """Widgets for the shop floor.

# Shipping

> Ship it today.

1. Pack the widget.
   Tape the box shut.
2. Call [`ship`](api.md#ship)

```python
ship(w)
```
"""
parts = md_parts(MD)
parts

Each Sent has the offsets of its sentence in the text. A newline always ends a sentence. md_parts keeps the spacing inside a line, which preserves the columns in a file of aligned rows. md_parts keeps each link, emphasis, HTML tag and formula whole inside its sentence, even a link target with spaces in it. The model sees them and can keep them in its rewrite:

FENCE = '`'*3
test_eq([(s and s.text, t) for s,t in parts], [('Widgets for the shop floor.', ''), (None, '# Shipping'), (None, '> Ship it today.'),
    ('Pack the widget.', '1. '), ('Tape the box shut.', ''), ('Call [`ship`](api.md#ship)', '2. '), (None, FENCE+'python\nship(w)\n'+FENCE)])
tape = parts[4][0]
test_eq(MD[tape.start:tape.end], 'Tape the box shut.')
test_eq([s.text for s,_ in md_parts('fork    exact clone\nagent   starts with nothing\n')], ['fork    exact clone', 'agent   starts with nothing'])
sp = 'Open [My Report.md](</a/My Project/My Report.md:3>)\n<span class="x">Then</span> close it.'
test_eq([s.text for s,_ in md_parts(sp)], ['Open [My Report.md](</a/My Project/My Report.md:3>)', '<span class="x">Then</span> close it.'])
test_eq([s.text for s,_ in md_parts('\\(x + y\\) is positive.\nThe total is \\(a + b\\)\n')], ['\\(x + y\\) is positive.', 'The total is \\(a + b\\)'])
test_eq(md_parts('# Sum \\(a + b\\)\nIt grows.')[0], (None, '# Sum \\(a + b\\)'))

title: rewrite
text:
Docstrings in a Python file
This source has a module docstring with a heading, a block quote and a numbered list. It also has a function with a one-line docstring, a method with an indented docstring of two paragraphs, and a method with none:

SRC = r'''"""Widgets for the shop floor.

# Shipping

`make` builds a widget. Finished widgets ride to the customer with `ship`.

> Ship it today.

1. Pack the widget.
2. Call `ship`.
"""
def make(spec):
    "Build a widget from `spec`"
    return Widget(spec)

class Widget:
    def __init__(self, spec): self.spec = spec
    def ship(self, addr):
        r"""Post the widget to `addr`.

        The label carries the order number. It raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.
        """
        if not addr: raise ValueError(addr)
'''

The docstrings to find belong to the module, its functions and its classes. _named walks the syntax tree and gives each function and class a dotted name, such as Widget.ship for a method. _doclit returns the string literal that is a node’s docstring, or None when the node has no docstring.

tree = ast.parse(SRC)
test_eq([nm for nm,_ in _named(tree)], ['make', 'Widget', 'Widget.__init__', 'Widget.ship'])
[(nm, bool(_doclit(n))) for nm,n in _docnodes(tree)]

py_docstrings returns each docstring of a Python source as a name, the text, and the offset of that text in the source. The module docstring comes first, with the name None. Each function and class follows in source order. A method has a dotted name such as Widget.ship. The text is taken from the file as written, between the quotes, because a rewrite is later put back at the same offsets.


source

py_docstrings
def py_docstrings(
    src
):
Each docstring in Python source src as (name, text, offset): the module’s first, with name None, then each function’s and class’s



ds = py_docstrings(SRC)
for nm,t,o in ds: test_eq(SRC[o:o+len(t)], t)
[(nm, t) for nm,t,o in ds]

The later lines of a docstring are usually indented to match the code around them. Markdown would read a paragraph indented by four spaces as code. _dedent removes the indentation that those lines share. It also returns a function that turns an offset in the result into the offset of the same character in the original:

d,back = _dedent('First.\n\n    Second line.\n    ')
test_eq(d, 'First.\n\nSecond line.\n')
test_eq(back(d.index('Second')), 12)
d

py_docs splits each docstring into the parts that md_parts returns. The offsets of each sentence are positions in the whole source.


source

py_docs
def py_docs(
    src
):
Each docstring of Python source src as (name, parts): parts are as md_parts returns, with sentence offsets that are positions in src



docs = py_docs(SRC)
docs

The second paragraph of the method’s docstring is found, though the file indents it. The offsets of each Sent are positions in the source file:

test_eq([nm for nm,_ in docs], [None, 'make', 'Widget.ship'])
raises = docs[2][1][2][0]
test_eq(raises.text, 'It raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.')
test_eq(SRC[raises.start:raises.end], 'It raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.')

title: rewrite
text:
The input for the model
rewrite_input writes the text that the model reads. Each docstring starts with a line that names it: Module docstring:, or the name of the function or class. Prose that is not a docstring has the name ''. It gets no such line in a Markdown file. A notebook’s code cells have the name CODE. Each is shown as fenced code with no number, and a Markdown cell: line marks the prose that follows it. Every sentence has a number in square brackets. The numbers do not restart for each docstring, because an answer names a sentence by its number alone. A list marker stays in front of the number of the sentence that starts the item. A line indented further than the first line of its paragraph is shown with that extra indentation after its number. Aligned rows then keep their columns. Headings, block quotes, code blocks and tables have no number.
A module can keep part of its docstring elsewhere and leave a {name} placeholder for it, as aai_coding.write_docs does. Pass that text in fills. The line after each sentence with a placeholder then gives the text that the placeholder stands for.


source

rewrite_input
def rewrite_input(
    docs, # (name, parts) pairs, as `file_docs` returns
    fills:NoneType=None, # Text that each `{name}` placeholder in the sentences stands for
    skip:NoneType=None, # Regex; a paragraph or list item that it matches gets `[-]` in place of each number
    nums:bool=True, # Number the sentences? False gives the same text with no numbers, as `_related` shows an earlier version
    mod_only:bool=False, # Give `[-]` to the docstrings of functions and classes? For a pyskill, whose module docstring is the skill's text
):
The text a model reads for docs: every sentence numbered unless skip matches its paragraph or mod_only excludes its docstring, with each docstring under a line that names it, and each code cell shown as context



inp = rewrite_input(docs)
print(inp)


for o in ('Module docstring:', '# Shipping', '> Ship it today.', '2. [4] Call `ship`.', 'Docstring of `Widget.ship`:', '[8] It raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.'):
    assert o in inp.splitlines()
test_eq(rewrite_input([('', parts)]).splitlines()[0], '[0] Widgets for the shop floor.')
filled = rewrite_input([('', md_parts('Avoid these.\n\n1. {hedging}'))], dict(hedging='Hedging. Say what is true.'))
test_eq(filled.splitlines()[-2:], ['1. [1] {hedging}', '  ({hedging} stands for: Hedging. Say what is true.)'])
test_eq(rewrite_input([('', md_parts('fork    exact clone\n        tell: its part\n'))]).splitlines(), ['[0] fork    exact clone', '[1]         tell: its part'])

Some lines are reference text that no model should rewrite, such as the line of key bindings at the top of each page of a manual. Pass skip, a regex, to leave them unnumbered. A paragraph or list item that skip matches gets [-] in place of each number, so the model reads it and has no number to answer with. The other sentences keep their numbers:

skipped = rewrite_input([('', parts)], skip=r'^Pack').splitlines()
for o in ('1. [-] Pack the widget.', '[-] Tape the box shut.', '2. [3] Call [`ship`](api.md#ship)'): assert o in skipped
skipped

A pyskill’s module docstring is the text of the skill, and its other docstrings document code. mod_only=True gives the sentences of those other docstrings [-], so the model reads them and does not rewrite them. nums=False leaves out every number. _related uses it to show an earlier version of a file in the same form as the document:

mo = rewrite_input(docs, mod_only=True).splitlines()
for o in ('[0] Widgets for the shop floor.', '[-] Build a widget from `spec`', '[-] The label carries the order number.'): assert o in mo
plain = rewrite_input(docs, nums=False)
assert '\n1. Pack the widget.' in plain and '[' not in plain
print(plain)

title: rewrite
text:
The model’s answer
The prompt asks for one answer per sentence. 7 - keeps sentence 7. 7 <text> replaces it. 7-8 <text> replaces sentences 7 and 8 together. 7 ? <question> asks what the sentence means. 7 ? cut: <why> and 7 ? lost: <fact> are questions too, so they need no parsing of their own. parse_rewrites reads those answers into (first, last, text) triples. It accepts the number with or without brackets. A line that starts with neither a number nor a space belongs to no answer, and it is skipped.


source

parse_rewrites
def parse_rewrites(
    reply
):
The answers of reply as (first, last, text) triples: text is - to keep the sentences, starts with ? for a question, and is otherwise the rewrite, without the > that a model may repeat from a description; indented lines under an answer are rows of its text



reply = """0 -
1 -
2 Call `ship` to post a finished widget to the customer.
[3] -
4 -
5 -
6 -
7 The order number is printed on the label.
8 ? what does it do when `addr` is only spaces"""
ans = parse_rewrites(reply)
test_eq(ans[2:4], [(2, 2, 'Call `ship` to post a finished widget to the customer.'), (3, 3, '-')])
test_eq(parse_rewrites('Here are my answers.\n5-6 One sentence for two.'), [(5, 6, 'One sentence for two.')])
ans[-2:]

A model can answer a run with rows, when a table or a list says it better than a sentence. It writes the number, then each row on a line of its own, indented. parse_rewrites keeps those lines in the answer. With no text beside the number, the rows are the whole answer:

rows = parse_rewrites("""3 -
4-6 Read through the kernel:
    file    `view_file`
    search  `rg`
7-8
    always        `ws-sync`
    code changed  restart
9 -""")
test_eq(rows[1], (4, 6, 'Read through the kernel:\n    file    `view_file`\n    search  `rg`'))
test_eq(rows[2], (7, 8, 'always        `ws-sync`\ncode changed  restart'))
rows[1:3]

section: Putting the rewrites into the source
text:
Putting the rewrites into the source
A rewrite must not damage the file. same_code makes a check for that. The check compares the syntax tree of a new source with the original’s and ignores what the docstrings say. A quotation mark that ends a docstring early is one way to fail it:


source

same_code
def same_code(
    src
):
A function that tells whether another source has the same code as Python source src, whatever its docstrings say



ok = same_code(SRC)
assert ok(SRC.replace('Build a widget', 'Make one widget'))
assert not ok(SRC.replace('return Widget(spec)', 'return None'))
assert not ok(SRC.replace('Build a widget', 'Build a "widget"'))

Rewrites applies the answers. Its new attribute is the source with each rewrite in place of the old sentence. rows lists every rewrite and question as (first, last, kind, old text, new text), for a person to review. missing counts the sentences that got no answer line. An answer that repeats its sentence unchanged counts as -.


source

Rewrites
def Rewrites(
    src, # The text that the sentence offsets are positions in
    docs, # (name, parts) pairs, as `py_docs` returns
    answers, # (first, last, text) triples, as `parse_rewrites` returns
    valid:NoneType=None, # Called with the source after each rewrite; a false result leaves that rewrite out
):


With the answers above, two sentences are rewritten. The rest of the file is as it was:

r = Rewrites(SRC, docs, ans, valid=same_code(SRC))
test_eq([(a, kind) for a,_,kind,*_ in r.rows], [(2, 'AFTER'), (7, 'AFTER'), (8, 'QUESTION')])
assert '`make` builds a widget. Call `ship` to post a finished widget to the customer.\n' in r.new
assert '        The order number is printed on the label. It raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.\n' in r.new
assert same_code(SRC)(r.new)
print(r.new)

of returns the rows of one kind. The display gives the counts, then each row as the old text and the new:


source

Rewrites.__repr__
def __repr__():
Return repr(self).




source

Rewrites.of
def of(
    kind
):
The rows of one kind: ‘AFTER’ for a rewrite made, ‘QUESTION’, or ‘LEFT OUT’ for a rewrite not made



test_eq(len(r.of('AFTER')), 2)
r

Rewrites leaves a rewrite out in three cases. Its range runs across two docstrings or two paragraphs. Another rewrite already covers one of its sentences. Or the valid check fails. Here the first answer joins a list item of the module docstring to the docstring of make, the second puts a double quotation mark into a docstring that double quotation marks enclose, and the last two both cover sentence 2:

out = Rewrites(SRC, docs, [(4, 5, 'Call `ship` and build a widget.'), (5, 5, 'Build a "widget" from `spec`'), (2, 2, 'Use `ship`.'), (1, 2, 'Use `make` and `ship`.')],
    valid=same_code(SRC))
test_eq([(a, b, kind) for a,b,kind,*_ in out.rows], [(1, 2, 'LEFT OUT'), (2, 2, 'AFTER'), (4, 5, 'LEFT OUT'), (5, 5, 'LEFT OUT')])
test_eq(out.missing, 5)
out

title: rewrite
text:
Notebooks
A notebook holds prose in its Markdown cells and docstrings in its code cells. nb_docs reads both in cell order. A Markdown cell gives its prose under the name ''. A code cell gives two things. Its whole source comes first under the name CODE, as context that the model reads and does not answer. The docstring of each function and class in it follows, numbered. A code cell that Python cannot parse, such as one with a magic, gives its source only. Raw cells and empty cells give nothing.
In an nbdev notebook the block quote under the title is the module’s description. nb_docs numbers its sentences so that the model reviews them, though other block quotes are context only. A description keeps its > marker in the model’s input. The prompt tells the model to keep such a sentence apart from the text after it, because listings show the description on its own.
A Rewrites works on one text. nb_docs therefore also returns the cell sources joined by SEP, and the sentence offsets are positions in that text. _addr gives each sentence an addr, the exhash address of the line it starts on:
A block quote directly under a title is the description of the page, so _md_parts numbers its sentences, whereas any other block quote is context. _cell_docs reads one cell, and nb_docs puts the cells together. In a notebook, a sentence’s addr starts with its cell ID:


source

nb_docs
def nb_docs(
    nb
):
The cell sources of notebook nb joined by SEP, and its (name, parts) pairs: the prose of each Markdown cell, and each code cell’s source followed by its docstrings; each sentence has its addr as cell ID and line address


This notebook has a title cell with a description, an exported function, a prose cell, a cell with a magic, and a raw cell:

NB = new_nb([mk_cell('# widgets\n\n> Build widgets and ship them to customers.', 'markdown'),
    mk_cell('#| export\ndef make(spec):\n    "Build a widget from `spec`"\n    return Widget(spec)'),
    mk_cell('`make` needs a spec. Finished widgets ride to the customer.', 'markdown'),
    mk_cell('%time make(1)'), mk_cell('Not prose.', 'raw')])
nsrc,ndocs = nb_docs(NB)
ndocs

In the input for the model, the description has its > marker, each code cell is fenced, and a Markdown cell: line marks where prose starts again. A model may repeat the > in its answer, and parse_rewrites drops it:

test_eq([nm for nm,_ in ndocs], ['', CODE, 'make', '', CODE])
desc = ndocs[0][1][1][0]
test_eq(nsrc[desc.start:desc.end], 'Build widgets and ship them to customers.')
test_eq(desc.addr, f'{NB.cells[0].id}:{lnhash_at(NB.cells[0].source, 3)}')
ninp = rewrite_input(ndocs)
assert '> [0] Build widgets and ship them to customers.' in ninp
assert '    return Widget(spec)\n```\n\nDocstring of `make`:\n\n[1] Build a widget from `spec`\n\nMarkdown cell:\n\n[2] `make` needs a spec.' in ninp
assert ninp.endswith('```python\n%time make(1)\n```')
test_eq(parse_rewrites('0 > Build and ship widgets.'), [(0, 0, 'Build and ship widgets.')])
print(ninp)

A rewrite in a notebook must leave the code of every code cell as it was. _same_cells makes that check for a SEP-joined text:

nok = _same_cells(NB)
nr = Rewrites(nsrc, ndocs, [(0, 0, 'Build widgets and ship them.'), (1, 1, 'Build a "widget"'), (3, 3, 'We send finished widgets to the customer.')], valid=nok)
test_eq([(a, kind) for a,_,kind,*_ in nr.rows], [(0, 'AFTER'), (1, 'LEFT OUT'), (3, 'AFTER')])
test_eq(nr.new.split(SEP)[0], '# widgets\n\n> Build widgets and ship them.')
nr

title: rewrite
text:
Rewriting a file
file_docs reads a file and returns what the later steps need: the text, the (name, parts) pairs, and the check that Rewrites runs after each rewrite. A notebook gives the text and pairs that nb_docs returns, with the _same_cells check. A .py file gives its docstrings and the same_code check. Any other file is read as Markdown and has no check. Its description is numbered too, as in the summary line under the title of an llms.txt file. Each sentence also gets an addr: the exhash address of the line it starts on, which in a notebook follows the cell ID.
write_new writes the new text of a Rewrites to a file. For a notebook it reads the notebook at path and replaces the source of each cell.


source

write_new
def write_new(
    path, new, dest:NoneType=None
):
Write new, the new text of a Rewrites for the file at path, to dest, or over path when dest is None; a notebook gets it as its cell sources and is validated first




source

file_docs
def file_docs(
    path
):
The text of the file at path, its (name, parts) pairs with a line address as each sentence’s addr, and a valid check for Rewrites: a notebook’s cells, a .py file’s docstrings, or the whole text of any other file



root = get_config().config_path
src,fdocs,valid = file_docs(root/'README.md')
test_eq([nm for nm,_ in fdocs], [''])
test_is(valid, None)
src,fdocs,valid = file_docs(root/'slopometer'/'score.py')
assert valid(src) and fdocs[0][0] is None
first = fdocs[0][1][0][0]
test_eq(first.addr, lnhash_at(src, src[:first.start].count('\n')+1))
first.addr

A Markdown file’s description is numbered, and a block quote further down is not. The description can follow the NB: line that a file for a language model has under its title. YAML front matter is shown without a number:

f = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'llms.txt'
f.write_text('---\nname: widgets\n---\n# Widgets\n\nNB: this file is designed for an LLM reader, not a human.\n\n> Widget API. Most shop idioms fail here.\n\n- make: `make(spec)`.\n\n> A later quotation.\n')
inp = rewrite_input(file_docs(f)[1]).splitlines()
for o in ('name: widgets', '> [1] Widget API.', '> [2] Most shop idioms fail here.', '> A later quotation.'): assert o in inp
inp

A notebook gives the check for its code cells, and each addr starts with a cell ID:

src,fdocs,valid = file_docs(root/'nbs'/'00_core.ipynb')
assert valid(src) and fdocs[0][1][1][0].addr.startswith(read_nb(root/'nbs'/'00_core.ipynb').cells[0].id+':')
rewrite_input(fdocs).splitlines()[:3]

prompt returns the prompt that ships with the package. It has a {document} placeholder where the numbered sentences go. The default prompt teaches full explanatory sentences. prompt('terse') is for reference pages written as short lines, such as the page for each primitive of an array language. It keeps the default prompt’s answer format and its last section, and has guidance and examples of its own between them. prompt('llm') is for files that a language model reads, such as an llms.txt file, a skill or a system prompt, written in the dense style that aai_coding.write_llms describes. Every style has two answers that are questions: ? cut: for a sentence that the reader does not need, and ? lost: for a fact that an earlier version has and this one lacks. _related writes out the files that a caller passes as context, for the model to consult. It puts the file passed as earlier last, under a heading that says it is an earlier version of the document. It shows that file as rewrite_input shows the document, without numbers. The model then compares like with like, and cannot report the code of a .py file as a fact that the docstrings have lost.


source

prompt
def prompt(
    style:NoneType=None, # Name of a style whose examples replace the default ones, `'terse'` or `'llm'`
):
The rewrite prompt that ships with the package, with a {document} placeholder for the numbered sentences


Pass a style’s prompt as template, as in rewrite_review(path, template=prompt('terse')). Every style shares the default prompt’s first and last sections, and the first has both question answers. The last lines check what _related writes for an earlier version. For a .py file that is its docstrings without numbers, and none of its code:

p,hdr = prompt(),'# The document'
for style in 'terse','llm':
    t = prompt(style)
    test_eq(t.split('\n# ')[0], p.split('\n# ')[0])
    test_eq(t.split(hdr)[1], p.split(hdr)[1])
assert 'Never turn a terse line into a longer sentence.' in prompt('terse')
for o in '? cut:','? lost:': assert o in p.split('\n# ')[0]
assert _related(None, f).startswith('\n\n# Earlier version of the document') and 'Widget API' in _related(None, f)
(py := f.with_suffix('.py')).write_text(SRC)
early = _related(None, py)
assert '`make` builds a widget.' in early and 'return Widget' not in early and '[1]' not in early

write_new(root/'slopometer'/'score.py', rw.new, '/tmp/score.rewritten.py')

title: rewrite
section: Two models, read by a person
text:
Two models, read by a person
A model’s rewrite is a suggestion. It can drop a fact, rename a term or split a sentence that was better whole. In this process the models only point at sentences, and a person or an agent reads what they said and writes the final text. compare prepares that reading. It takes each model’s answers under the model’s name. The first line counts the sentences, and for each model the runs it rewrote and the questions it asked. Answers whose sentence ranges overlap are grouped into one run. For each run, it gives the address of the first sentence, the original text, and then each model’s answer. Models whose answers differ only in case, spacing or punctuation share a line. A model that kept the sentences shows -.
With now, the sentences of the file after editing, each run also gets a NOW: line with the text that stands there. NOW: - means that the run reads as it did.
_now finds what stands in the edited file where each run of original sentences was. It lines up the two lists of sentences with difflib and returns None for a run that reads as it did.
compare builds the text:


source

compare
def compare(
    docs, # (name, parts) pairs of the original, as `file_docs` returns
    answers, # Each model's name with its answers, as `parse_rewrites` returns them
    now:NoneType=None, # The sentences of the file after editing
    code:bool=False, # Show a notebook's code cell under the first run that explains it?
    brief:bool=False, # Keep only the runs that a model asked about or that every model changed?
    pending:bool=False, # Keep only the runs that read as they did before editing? Needs `now`
):
Text for review: counts, then each run of sentences in docs that a model changed, with its address, the original, each answer, and with now what stands there after editing


Here a second model answers the same file as ans above. It joins sentences 1 and 2, keeps sentence 7 and repeats sentence 4 unchanged, which counts as keeping it:

ans2 = parse_rewrites("""1-2 `make` builds a widget and `ship` posts it to the customer.
4 Call `ship`.
7 -""")
cmp = compare(docs, dict(first=ans, second=ans2))
assert '1-2 ORIGINAL: `make` builds a widget. Finished widgets ride to the customer with `ship`.\n  FIRST [2]: Call `ship` to post' in cmp
assert '  SECOND [1-2]: `make` builds a widget and `ship` posts it to the customer.' in cmp
assert '7 ORIGINAL: The label carries the order number.\n  FIRST [7]: The order number is printed on the label.\n  SECOND: -' in cmp
assert '4 ORIGINAL' not in cmp
print(cmp)

A long comparison is quicker to read in two passes. brief=True keeps only the runs that a model asked a question about or that every model changed. Here the second model kept sentence 7, so that run is left out:

short = compare(docs, dict(first=ans, second=ans2), brief=True)
assert short.startswith('9 sentences.') and 'Shown: 2 of 3 runs.' in short and '7 ORIGINAL' not in short
print(short)

A file’s review files go to one folder, which is review_dir(path) under XDG state unless you pass out. The folder keeps the orig copy, which is the file before its first review. Each review then writes to a numbered folder of its own inside that folder, 1 for the first review. A later review therefore keeps the replies of the earlier ones. A numbered folder holds the reviewed copy, which is the file as that review numbered it, and the input, the replies and the comparison.


source

review_dir
def review_dir(
    path
):
The folder under XDG state that holds the review files for the file at path


_answers reads the replies that one review saved. _numbers_ok checks that this version of the package numbers the file’s sentences as that review did, because a reply’s numbers mean nothing otherwise:
rewrite_review asks each model in asks about one file, all at once, with no system message. ASKS names the two models we use and the reasoning effort for each. It changes nothing in the file itself. It saves a copy of the file, the numbered input, each model’s reply as returned, and the comparison, which it also returns. Give it a list of files and it reviews them together and returns one comparison for each.
review_diff compares the file with the orig copy, and a later review of the same file leaves that copy alone unless you pass fresh=True. When the file differs from that copy, a later review also gives the copy to the models as the earlier version, so that they can answer ? lost: for a fact that an edit dropped. Pass earlier to name another file, such as the original of a file that you edited before its first review. The sentence numbers in review_apply and review_report are those of the latest review, unless you pass n to name an earlier one.
fills, skip and mod_only go to rewrite_input. Pass mod_only=True for a pyskill. Pass context to give the models files to consult, such as the code that a Markdown document describes. Their contents follow the document in the prompt. A long comparison is quicker to read in two passes. brief=True returns only the runs that a model asked a question about or that every model changed, and the whole comparison is still written to the folder. code=True prints each notebook code cell under the first run that explains it.


source

rewrite_review
async def rewrite_review(
    path, # File to review, or a list of them: Markdown, a notebook, or a `.py` file for its docstrings
    out:NoneType=None, # Folder to write to; `review_dir(path)` if None
    template:NoneType=None, # Prompt with a `{document}` placeholder; `prompt()` if None
    asks:dict={'carbon': ('gemini/models/gemini-4-carbon', 'low'), 'sol': ('gpt-6.1-sol', 'medium')}, # Name of each answer and its (model, effort)
    fills:NoneType=None, # Text that each `{name}` placeholder in the sentences stands for
    context:NoneType=None, # Files that the models can consult, such as the code that a document describes
    code:bool=False, # Show each notebook code cell under the first run that explains it?
    brief:bool=False, # Return only the runs that a model asked about or that every model changed?
    fresh:bool=False, # Save the file as a new original? The original that it replaces moves into the folder of the latest review
    skip:NoneType=None, # Regex; a paragraph or list item that it matches gets `[-]` in place of each number
    earlier:NoneType=None, # File that holds an earlier version, for `? lost:` answers; the original that the first review saved if None and the file has changed since
    mod_only:bool=False, # Give `[-]` to the docstrings of functions and classes? For a pyskill, whose module docstring is the skill's text
):
Ask each model in asks about the file at path; write the original to out, and a copy of the file, the input, each reply and their compare text to a new numbered folder in out; return that text, or one text for each file of a list; brief shortens what is returned, not what is written


With GEMINI_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY set, review one file:

print(await rewrite_review(root/'README.md'))

Here the two sets of answers above have reviewed a file, and one sentence has since been edited by hand. The review folder holds the original. Its folder 1 holds the first review’s copy of the file and both replies, as rewrite_review would have written them:

f,out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'widgets.py',Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(out/'widgets.orig.py').write_text(SRC)
(d1 := out/'1').mkdir()
(d1/'widgets.reviewed.py').write_text(SRC)
(d1/'widgets.first.answer.txt').write_text(reply)
(d1/'widgets.second.answer.txt').write_text('1-2 `make` builds a widget and `ship` posts it to the customer.\n7 the order number is printed on the label')
f.write_text(SRC.replace('The label carries the order number.', 'The order number is printed on the label.'))

review_apply makes the edits for you. Give it the new text for each sentence, keyed by the sentence’s number in the comparison, by a (first, last) pair for a run, or by the old text itself. Numbers are those of the latest review, or of review n, and they still work after earlier edits have moved the sentences. An old text can be one sentence or a run of neighbouring ones, and it must occur exactly once. The call finds the cell and line itself. It writes nothing unless every edit can be made: a number that names a sentence you have already edited, an old text that is missing, and an edit that would change code each raise a ValueError that lists every failure. A notebook is validated before it is written. Numbers from a review that an older version of the package made can name the wrong sentences. The call refuses those too, and old texts still work as keys.


source

review_apply
def review_apply(
    path, # File to edit
    edits, # New text for each sentence or run, or an empty one to delete it; a key is a number or (first, last) pair from the comparison, or the old text itself
    out:NoneType=None, # Folder that `rewrite_review` wrote to; `review_dir(path)` if None
    n:NoneType=None, # Review whose numbers the keys use, counting from 1; the latest if None
):
Put each new text of edits into the file at path in place of the sentences that its key names; if any edit cannot be made, raise ValueError that lists them all, and write nothing


Here one call replaces the run of sentences 1 and 2, using their numbers from the comparison:

msg = review_apply(f, {(1, 2): '`make` builds a widget and `ship` posts it to the customer.'}, out)
assert '`make` builds a widget and `ship` posts it to the customer.\n' in f.read_text()
msg

Sentence 7 was edited by hand above, so its number no longer names a sentence in the file. The call fails, and the edit beside it is not written either:

before = f.read_text()
test_fail(lambda: review_apply(f, {7: 'Labels have order numbers.', 'Call `ship`.': 'Then call `ship`.'}, out), contains='7: not in the review, or edited since')
test_eq(f.read_text(), before)

An empty new text deletes the sentences that its key names. review_apply also removes the space between them and the next sentence of their paragraph, or else the space after the previous sentence. It removes space on the same line first, which leaves each aligned row on its own line. When a paragraph or list item loses every sentence, review_apply removes its lines and leaves no extra blank line. This file has no review. Its keys are numbers in the file as it stands:

MDX = 'Alpha one. Beta two. Gamma three.\nDelta four.\n\n- Item one.\n- Item two.\n  Item two more.\n\nx   row one. row two.\ny   row three.\n'
md = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'notes.md'
def cut(*ks):
    md.write_text(MDX)
    review_apply(md, {k: '' for k in ks}, md.parent/'reviews')
    return md.read_text()
test_eq(cut(1).splitlines()[0], 'Alpha one. Gamma three.')
test_eq(cut(0).splitlines()[0], 'Beta two. Gamma three.')
test_eq(cut(2, 3), MDX.replace(' Gamma three.\nDelta four.', ''))
test_eq(cut(4), MDX.replace('- Item one.\n', ''))
test_eq(cut(5), MDX.replace('Item two.\n  ', ''))
test_eq(cut(8), MDX.replace(' row two.', ''))
test_eq(cut(7, 8), MDX.replace('x   row one. row two.\n', ''))
test_eq(cut(4, 5, 6), MDX.replace('- Item one.\n- Item two.\n  Item two more.\n\n', ''))
P = 'Para one.\n\nB.\n\nPara three.\n'
test_eq([Rewrites(P, [('', md_parts(P))], [(k, k, '')]).new for k in range(3)], ['B.\n\nPara three.\n', 'Para one.\n\nPara three.\n', 'Para one.\n\nB.\n'])
print(cut(2, 3, 5))

review_diff lists what you changed, by hand or with review_apply. It compares the file with the original that the first review saved.


source

review_diff
def review_diff(
    path, # File that was reviewed and then edited
    out:NoneType=None, # Folder that `rewrite_review` wrote to; `review_dir(path)` if None
    n:NoneType=None, # Show only what changed during review `n`, counting from 1; every change since the first review if None
):
What differs between the original that the first review saved and the file at path now, or with n what changed during one review: the file’s name, then each changed sentence or heading under its address, as - lines and the + lines that replace them


The diff starts with the file’s name and the number of changes. Each change has the address of the text as it now stands, and a note when the text is a docstring or in an exported Markdown cell, since a module generated from the file then needs exporting again. The two sentences that became one are shown together:

dif = review_diff(f, out)
assert dif.startswith(f'# {f}: 2 changes')
assert '(module docstring)\n- `make` builds a widget.\n- Finished widgets ride to the customer with `ship`.\n+ `make` builds a widget and `ship` posts it to the customer.' in dif
assert f'@{lnhash_at(f.read_text(), 21)} (docstring of `Widget.ship`)\n- The label carries the order number.\n+ The order number is printed on the label.' in dif
print(dif)

review_report writes the comparison again with a NOW: line for each run, which shows the answers you took and those you left. It reports on the latest review, or on review n. It reads that review’s copy of the file and its replies, and writes the report beside them. It returns the counts and the report’s file name, because the whole text is long. Pass full=True to get the text.


source

review_report
def review_report(
    path, # File that was reviewed and then edited
    out:NoneType=None, # Folder that `rewrite_review` wrote to; `review_dir(path)` if None
    full:bool=False, # Return the whole report, not only its counts and where it is?
    code:bool=False, # Show each notebook code cell under the first run that explains it?
    brief:bool=False, # Keep only the runs that a model asked about or that every model changed?
    n:NoneType=None, # Review to report on, counting from 1; the latest if None
):
Write the compare text of one review of the file at path, with what each run of sentences reads after editing, to that review’s folder; return its counts and the file’s name, or the text with full


The report starts with the counts. Sentence 7 is on line 22 of the file, both models gave the same rewrite for it, and it was taken. So was the second model’s answer for sentences 1 and 2. The last run reads as it did:

rep = review_report(f, out, full=True)
assert rep.startswith('9 sentences. FIRST: 2 rewritten, 1 asked. SECOND: 2 rewritten, 0 asked. Edited: 2 of 3 runs.')
assert f"7 @{lnhash_at(SRC, 21)} ORIGINAL: The label carries the order number.\n  FIRST, SECOND [7]: The order number is printed on the label.\n  NOW: The order number is printed on the label." in rep
test_eq(rep.count('  NOW: -'), 1)
print(rep)
review_report(f, out)

Each review has a numbered folder of its own, so a second review keeps the replies of the first. Here a second review of the edited file has one reply with two rewrites, and review_apply puts in one of them:

(d2 := out/'2').mkdir()
(d2/'widgets.reviewed.py').write_text(f.read_text())
(d2/'widgets.third.answer.txt').write_text('0 Widgets for a shop floor.\n7 `ship` raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.')
review_apply(f, {7: '`ship` raises `ValueError` when `addr` is empty.'}, out)

review_diff with n shows what changed during one review. n counts the reviews from 1, and a negative n counts back from the latest:

dif2 = review_diff(f, out, n=2)
assert dif2.startswith(f'# {f}: 1 change during review 2') and 'order number' not in dif2
assert '2 changes during review 1' in review_diff(f, out, n=1)
test_eq(review_diff(f, out, n=-1), dif2)
print(dif2)

review_pending goes through every review. For each one it lists the runs that a model rewrote or asked about and that still read as they did in that review. Use it to find suggestions that nobody has acted on.


source

review_pending
def review_pending(
    path, # File that has been reviewed
    out:NoneType=None, # Folder that `rewrite_review` wrote to; `review_dir(path)` if None
    code:bool=False, # Show each notebook code cell under the first run that explains it?
):
For each review of the file at path, the runs that a model rewrote or asked about and that still read as they did in that review: one compare text under a heading for each review


Every run of the first review has been edited since. In the second review, nobody has acted on the rewrite of sentence 0:

pend = review_pending(f, out)
r1,r2 = pend.split('# Review 2\n')
assert r1.startswith('# Review 1\n') and 'Shown: 0 of 3 runs.' in r1
assert 'Shown: 1 of 2 runs.' in r2 and 'ORIGINAL: Widgets for the shop floor.' in r2 and 'addr' not in r2
print(pend)

The models miss sentences. A docstring can read clearly beside the prose that explains it and still be unclear on its own. review_passed lists the sentences of one review that no model rewrote or asked about, without the code, for a person or an agent to read. It leaves out the sentences that the models read without a number, which mod_only and skip mark [-]. Each has the number that review_apply takes and its address. A line names each docstring above its sentences.


source

review_passed
def review_passed(
    path, # File that has been reviewed
    out:NoneType=None, # Folder that `rewrite_review` wrote to; `review_dir(path)` if None
    n:NoneType=None, # Review to read, counting from 1; the latest if None
):
The numbered sentences that no model rewrote or asked about in one review of the file at path: a count, then each as its number, address and text, with a line that names each docstring


In the first review, the two models between them rewrote or asked about sentences 1, 2, 7 and 8. The other five are listed:

psd = review_passed(f, out, n=1)
assert psd.startswith('5 of 9 sentences that no model changed in review 1.')

title: pangram
text:
pangram_text and pangram_path send prose to Pangram’s AI-detection API instead of running the rules. They read the same Markdown as score_text and score_path. They return a Result with the same addresses, JSON fields and min_words cutoff. slopometer --pangram runs pangram_path from the command line.
Pangram scores text in windows, which can run to hundreds of words. Each finding is one window. Its weight is the window’s score multiplied by 10. A window that Pangram rates fully AI-written weighs 10, the same as a kill-tier rule finding. The density is the mean window score, weighted by word count, on a scale from 0 (human) to 100 (AI). Under --pangram, --threshold compares against this scale.
Each request sends the text to Pangram’s servers and costs about $0.05 per 100 words. The functions read the API key from PANGRAM_API_KEY.
import json
from fastcore.test import *
from nbdev.config import get_config

title: pangram
text:
What Pangram reads
Pangram reads the blocks the rules read: headings, list items and paragraphs, with code removed. _pangram_input joins them with single newlines and returns each block’s offset in the joined text. Pangram collapses each blank line to one newline before it reports window offsets. With single newlines, its offsets match the text sent.

sent, offs = _pangram_input(segment(t2))
for b,o in zip(segment(t2), offs): test_eq(sent[o:o+len(b.txt)], b.txt)
sent[:200]

title: pangram
text:
Calling Pangram
Pangram runs each request as a task. _predict posts the text to /task, then polls /task/{id} every half second until the task’s stage is STAGE_SUCCESS or STAGE_FAILED. It returns Pangram’s response as a dict. It raises an error when the task fails or takes longer than timeout seconds.
samples/theory2.pangram.json holds Pangram’s response for samples/theory2.md. The examples below read it, so they run without an API key or network access. This cell recorded it:

(sd/'theory2.pangram.json').write_text(json.dumps(_predict(sent), indent=1))

Density is the mean window score, weighted by word count and scaled to 0-100. A 300-word window scored 1.0 and a 100-word window scored 0.0 give a score of 75:

The label-side scorer
The rules select the positives, and the forest’s features must stay independent of that selection. Most features are safe by construction: burstiness, sentence lengths, part-of-speech rates, specifics density, and the referential measures share no vocabulary with any rule. Assembly
build_corpus fetches every source, scores each row with label_density, applies the cuts, and writes two files under XDG state: corpus.jsonl for training and eval.jsonl for the complaint labels, which training must never read. The middle band joins neither side. Measured on this machine, reply densities run 31/64/124 at the 10th/50th/90th percentile, and the human sources run far lower but not at zero: your own long requests reach a median of 37, because genuine questions and dash habits fire rules there too. The default cuts come from those distributions and from reading rows at the boundaries: 50 admits seven in ten replies as confident slop, and 30 admits about half of the human paragraphs. title: score
text:
Referential load, a prototype
Splitting sentences can leave references unclear. “It reads the same stdin” needs an antecedent for “it”. “The record of completed imports dies with the process” assumes the reader knows which record. Entity-based coherence models, such as Barzilay and Lapata (2008), study how documents introduce entities and refer to them later.
refload measures two possible indicators:

The pronoun rate (pron) is the fraction of sentences whose main subject is a pronoun.
The cold-definite rate (cold) is the fraction of “the X” phrases where X has not appeared earlier in the document. This count excludes “the same X” and placeholder tokens used for inline code.

These are experimental measurements, not scoring rules.

def refload(txt):
    n_sent = n_pron = n_def = n_cold = 0
    seen = set()
    for d in (x for x in parse_blocks(segment(txt)) if x is not None):
        for s in d.sents:
            n_sent += 1
            if any(t.dep_ in ('nsubj', 'nsubjpass') and t.pos_ == 'PRON' and t.head.dep_ == 'ROOT' for t in s): n_pron += 1
        for t in d:
            if t.pos_ not in ('NOUN', 'PROPN') or len(set(t.lower_)) == 1: continue
            lem = t.lemma_.lower()
            kids = [c.lower_ for c in t.children]
            if 'the' in kids and 'same' not in kids:
                n_def += 1
                if lem not in seen: n_cold += 1
            seen.add(lem)
    return dict(sents=n_sent, pron=round(n_pron/max(n_sent, 1), 2), defs=n_def, cold=round(n_cold/max(n_def, 1), 2))


texts = {f'theory{i}': (sd/f'theory{i}.md').read_text() for i in (1, 2, 3, 4)} | dict(AFTER=AFTER, BEFORE=BEFORE)

title: core
text:
slopometer measures prose against the reference-prose rules in aai_coding.write_docs: 19 numbered tells, the named ways reference prose goes wrong. This module defines what every rule shares: the table of tells, the Finding record every detector returns, the registry that rules join at import time, and the registry of tells no deterministic rule can detect.
from fastcore.test import *

title: core
text:
The tells
The numbers are write_docs’s own, and its docstring stays the source for what each tell means. They are append-only, so a rule bound to a number stays correct across revisions. slopometer names the tells and never restates them. Rules built on write_docs guidance that sits outside the numbered tells, like the banned-word lists and the active-voice preference, carry tell=None and display without a tell clause. advice holds a short instruction for each tell whose findings agents tend to fix mechanically. A finding for that tell carries the instruction and prints it after the flagged text.

title: core
text:
Findings
The tiers span an order of magnitude on purpose. One kill-on-sight finding outweighs any accumulation of pressure findings. Calibration against the write_docs passage pair will set the exact numbers. The tiers are the commitment.


source

Finding
def Finding(
    rule, # Name of the rule that fired
    tell, # `write_docs` tell number the rule detects
    start, # Character offset where the span starts, within the text the detector received
    end, # Character offset one past the span's end
    text, # The offending span itself
    weight, # The rule's tier, escalated where the rule escalates
    suggestion:NoneType=None, # A mechanical replacement, when one exists
):


A Finding is one rule firing on one span. start and end are offsets into the text the detector received. The runner rebases them to file positions when it assembles a report. The span text is stored too, and a finding therefore displays without its source. Here is a finding built by hand, for the sentence the meter exists to catch:

s = "It isn't just a poller - it's the liveness authority."
Finding('notxbuty', 14, 0, len(s), s, KILL)

Rules join rules at import time through the decorator, which stamps the metadata that the runner and the drift test read. A detector receives one unit of text at its level and nothing wider. That locality is a design rule from the PRD: the paragraph is the largest unit of linguistic analysis.
The simplest rule in the package needs no parse and no lexicon, and it serves here as the registry’s working example: tell 18, decoration. Reference prose is ASCII. Emoji and ornamental symbols are always wrong in it, which makes this a kill-on-sight rule, and arrow glyphs get a mechanical suggestion. Accented letters are ordinary spelling, not decoration. The em dash marks a tacked-on clause (tell 1), not decoration, and a different rule owns it. What the meter cannot see
Six entries record judgment no deterministic rule reaches. Recording them with reasons serves two consumers. The drift test in the scoring notebook asserts that every write_docs tell number maps to a rule or to an entry here, and a tell added to write_docs without a slopometer decision fails it.
